orders.description: Cattaraugus County order entered May 9, 2016, on Krotz’s motion
orders.trial_court_action: Denied summary judgment dismissing the amended complaint and cross claims against the snowplowing contractor.

facts.factual_summary: Lingenfelter allegedly slipped on snow and ice between parking spaces in an apartment complex’s lot. The owners hired Krotz for snowplowing. Krotz plowed the central driving lane and did not remove snow between the parking spaces.

legal_issues.finding: Krotz’s snowplowing obligations arose from its contract with the owners. The contract and performance did not establish a duty to Lingenfelter.
Plowing the central lane did not create or exacerbate the condition between the parking spaces, and Lingenfelter failed to raise a triable issue on that theory.

Krotz did not create or worsen the hazard, Lingenfelter did not rely on continued performance, and the property manager retained oversight. The agreement did not displace the owners’ maintenance duty.
The third Espinal exception had not been pleaded, so the contractor was not required to negate it. The court nevertheless found the exception inapplicable.
The court also dismissed the owners’ cross claim against Krotz for contribution and indemnification.

evidence_discussed.description: The snowplowing agreement defined Krotz’s obligations and the property manager’s continuing oversight.
The court considered the property manager’s deposition and the contractor owner’s deposition and affidavit.

quality.notes: The order reversed the denial of one motion and dismissed the direct injury claim and the cross claim against Krotz. No appellate disposition concerning other defendants is implied.

evidence.quote: Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Cattaraugus County (Jeremiah J. Moriarty, III, J.), entered May 9, 2016. The order denied the motion of defendant William Krotz Contracting for summary judgment dismissing the amended complaint and all cross claims against it.

It is hereby ordered that the order so appealed from is unanimously reversed on the law without costs, the motion is granted, and the amended complaint and the cross claim against defendant William Krotz Contracting are dismissed.

Plaintiff commenced this action seeking damages for injuries she allegedly sustained when she slipped and fell on ice and snow between parking spaces in the parking lot of an apartment complex owned and operated by defendants Delevan Terrace Associates, Cattaraugus Community Action, Inc., and Cattaraugus Rural Housing Corporation (collectively, apartment defendants).
The apartment defendants contracted with defendant William Krotz Contracting (Krotz) to provide snowplowing services for the property.
On appeal, Krotz contends that Supreme Court erred in denying its motion for summary judgment seeking dismissal of the amended complaint and any cross claims against it. We agree.
any duty that Krotz had with respect to snowplowing on the subject property arose exclusively out of its contract with the apartment defendants
we conclude that Krotz met its initial burden of establishing that it did not launch a force or instrument of harm by creating or exacerbating a dangerous condition

Krotz’s submissions, including the contract, the deposition testimony of the property manager for the apartment complex, and the deposition testimony and affidavit of Krotz’s owner, established that Krotz plowed the center driving lane of the parking lot in accordance with its responsibilities under the contract and did not undertake any snow removal operations with respect to the condition between the parking spaces that caused plaintiff’s injury.
Plaintiff failed to raise an issue of fact whether Krotz negligently created or exacerbated a dangerous condition
It is undisputed that plaintiff did not detrimentally rely on Krotz’s continued performance of its contractual obligations, and thus the second Espinal exception cannot form a basis for liability

Krotz was not required to negate the third Espinal exception inasmuch as there are no allegations in the pleadings that would establish the applicability of that exception, i.e., that Krotz entirely displaced the apartment defendants’ duty to maintain the premises safely

while the contract provided Krotz with some discretion in fulfilling its snowplowing obligations, its terms made Krotz directly responsible to the property manager who had the right to request additional services and oversaw maintenance of the property, including snowplowing

the contract between [Krotz] and the [apartment defendants] was not so comprehensive and exclusive that it entirely displaced the [apartment defendants’] duty to maintain the premises safely, such that [Krotz] owed a duty to plaintiff”
Finally, we agree with Krotz that the court erred in denying its motion insofar as it sought dismissal of the apartment defendants’ cross claim for contribution and indemnification

orders.trial_court_action: Granted Sanchez summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Caicedo’s daughter said her mother took two or three steps and slipped down basement stairs in a mixed-use building with a medical office downstairs and a residence upstairs. The daughter could not identify what Caicedo slipped on.

legal_issues.finding: The owner’s safe-maintenance duty extended to hazards of which she had notice. The record did not establish notice, and inherent slipperiness alone was insufficient.
There was no evidence of a prior injury or complaint about the floor to support notice.
The record did not support a finding that Sanchez should have known of the allegedly hazardous condition.

Caicedo could not describe the accident. Her daughter did not identify a slippery condition or explain how Caicedo reached the basement stairs from the procedure room. The alleged connection between the tiles and the fall lacked support.
The expert measured tile friction and opined that the result was unsafe. The court held that inherent slipperiness alone could not sustain the negligence claim.

evidence_discussed.description: Sanchez testified about the building layout. Caicedo could not supply an account when her deposition was attempted.
Caicedo’s daughter described the slip but could not say what caused it.
The owner referred to an exterior photograph and the daughter identified the procedure room from a photograph.
The expert reported a drag-sled friction reading of 0.36 and considered a reading below 0.50 unsafe.

quality.notes: The daughter expressly described a slip, so uncertainty about the cause does not eliminate the incident from scope. The court did not accept the expert’s threshold as establishing liability.

evidence.quote: Order, Supreme Court, Bronx County (Lizbeth Gonzalez, J.), entered August 28, 2012, which granted defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, unanimously affirmed, without costs.

Plaintiff Honoria Caicedo sustained injury on May 28, 2006 when she fell down the basement stairs on premises owned by defendant Janet Sanchez, M.D., a two-story structure containing a medical office on the first floor and a residential apartment on the second.

Although he had been instructed not to allow anyone else onto the premises, Hugo invited third-party defendant Maria Torres to stay with him. She arrived, accompanied by her son and daughter and plaintiff, her mother, in the early evening of May 27, 2006.

an attempt to depose her in October 2009 was abandoned when she could not remember the accident, did not recall having been injured and did not recognize Maria Torres, who had brought her to the deposition.

Sanchez gave deposition testimony in which she described the layout of the premises. Referring to a photograph of the exterior, which depicts two doors, she identified the right door as the main entrance to her office and the left as the entrance leading to her apartment.
At the back of the waiting room is a door to a room used to take blood and to the immediate left is the door to the basement stairs, which is kept locked.

Maria Torres testified that, upon arriving at the premises, she and her family used the left entrance door to go into the procedure room, where a bed had been set up for her mother. She identified the room from a photograph as the procedure room.
Ms. Torres stated that her mother rose, took two or three steps, and slipped and fell down the basement stairs.
She could not state what, if anything, her mother had slipped on and had not noticed that the floor was slippery.

Plaintiff offered the affidavit of an expert who tested the floor tiles. Using a drag sled to measure the coefficient of friction, the expert obtained a reading of 0.36. He opined that any reading of less than 0.50 is indicative of an unsafe condition.

Plaintiff failed to explain how she took two or three steps from a chair in the procedure room and slipped and fell down the basement stairs that were located in the back of the adjacent waiting room.
Maria Torres conceded that she did not know what caused her mother to fall and had not noticed that the floor was slippery.
Finally, there is no evidence of any prior injury or complaint about the floor to support the conclusion that Dr. Sanchez should have known about the allegedly hazardous condition

Proof that a floor is “inherently slippery,” standing alone, is insufficient to support a cause of action for negligence (Waiters v Northern Trust Co. of N.Y., 29 AD3d 325, 326-327 [1st Dept 2006]; Kruimer v National Cleaning Contrs., 256 AD2d 1 [1st Dept 1998]), and the complaint was properly dismissed.

orders.description: Bronx County order entered on or about May 31, 2016
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Peña slipped at a building owned by 2305 Grandco and managed by Tyrax. The superintendent said he had mopped the area with soap and water about five minutes before the fall and had not placed warning signs.

legal_issues.finding: The superintendent’s account raised a factual question whether defendants created the condition through recent mopping without warning signs.
Peña’s testimony provided a nonspeculative link between the alleged condition and her fall.
Any hearsay in the recorded conversation could be considered with the other evidence when deciding whether the opposition defeated summary judgment.

evidence_discussed.description: The superintendent described when he mopped and the lack of warning signs.
The court credited Peña’s account as sufficient to link the condition to the fall at this stage.
The recorded conversation contained a Tyrax manager’s acknowledgment of mopping without subsequent warnings.

quality.notes: Potential duplicate decision with C_020 NY-4389907: same parties, appellate date, appealed order and accident evidence. Preserve both manifest IDs and flag them together for case-family review before splitting or counting independent decisions.

evidence.quote: Order, Supreme Court, Bronx County (Fernando Tapia, J.), entered on or about May 31, 2016, which denied defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, unanimously affirmed, without costs.

Defendants failed to make a prima facie showing of their entitlement to summary judgment, since the evidence they submitted raises genuine issues of fact about whether they created a dangerous condition

The superintendent of the building owned by defendant 2305 Grandco and managed by defendant Tyrax testified that he had mopped the accident location with soap and water approximately five minutes before plaintiff slipped and fell and did not place warning signs in the area.
plaintiff’s testimony provides a non-speculative basis for her version of the accident and sufficiently establishes a nexus between the hazardous condition and the circumstances of her fall
the transcript of a recorded conversation between plaintiff and a Tyrax manager, in which the manager conceded that the area had been mopped and that no warning signs were placed thereafter.
Even if a portion of the transcript is hearsay, under the particular circumstances it *441 may be considered in conjunction with the other evidence to defeat summary judgment
